competencies.statement: I can launch parachutes from a stand; see which parachute falls the slowest.
competencies.explanation: The Scout, with other Scouts should drop their parachutes and see which falls to the ground fastest. After the activity the Scout should be able to point out the reasons why.

competencies.statement: I can discuss with my Scouter how the wind affects a parachute.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should show an awareness of the affect of wind on a parachute. In particular they should mention drifting and land and air speed, into and against the wind.

competencies.statement: I know what you should do if somebody gets hurt.
competencies.explanation: The Scout needs to show an ability to recognize that someone is hurt badly and needs help. The Scout should also know how to get help and by what means. How to discover that someone is hurt. How to compare injured parts with uninjured parts. Methods of getting help. Methods of caring for someone that is hurt.

competencies.statement: I know the safe way to act at an airport and can discuss this with my Scouter.
competencies.explanation: Scouts should understand the difference between the restricted areas of an airfield where active aircraft movements can be expected and the safe public areas. They should also be able to recognise the signs and markings which indicate the boundary between the two areas.

competencies.statement: I can build a Kite and fly it.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should present a kite he/she has made and be ready to fly it. The flight should be observed and if possible be part of an air scouting activity.

competencies.statement: I know where it would be safe to fly a kite.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know where it is safe to fly a kite. He/she should discuss suitable and unsuitable areas and the features that make an area unsafe.

competencies.statement: I know the difference between airside and landside.
competencies.explanation: Scouts should be able to explain how a modern airport is laid out. The Scout should understand the difference between ‘airside’ and ‘landside’ and the necessary precautions and procedures that are required in each area.

competencies.statement: I can discuss the first flight by the Wright Bros.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should have done some research and be able to discuss the Wright Brothers impact on air travel.

competencies.statement: I know the main parts of an aero plane.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should list the main parts of an aircraft by marking the names on a diagram: Fuselage/ Body.Cockpit. Wing., Tail/ Fin., Tailplane. Engines. Undercarriage.

competencies.statement: I know the rules of safety around an aero plane.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain how to behave around an aircraft. How to approach it. How to observe movement. The areas to avoid front and back. Following the instructions of the pilot and the Scouter in charge.

competencies.statement: I can discuss why communication is important to aircraft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should display his/her knowledge about how important communications are in air flight. Air traffic control, communication of position, flight plans etc. should be mentioned.

competencies.statement: I know the phonetic alphabet.
competencies.explanation: Scouts should know the phonetic alphabet used in radio communications, i.e. Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, etc.

competencies.statement: I can name the planets in our Solar System.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to name of all of the planets in the Solar System and know what order they come in relation to distance from the Sun.

competencies.statement: I know the main points of ‘Leave no Trace and why it’s important at airports.
competencies.explanation: In addition to the points below, Scouts should have a special understanding of the dangers to aviation of having waste material or other items blowing around an airfield where they may get sucked into engines, block air intakes or otherwise cause damage to aircraft. Food waste in particular may attract birds which represent a particular hazard to aircraft operating near to the ground. Scouts should demonstrate an understanding of the key points in a practical way in a camp situation. Dispose of waste properly. Respect farm animals and wildlife. Minimise camping impact and the effects of fire. Be considerate of others. Travel and camp on durable surfaces. Leave what you find. Plan ahead and prepare.

competencies.statement: I have built a scale model aircraft to a satisfactory standard from a plastic kit and can explain its features and history.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should present a model he/she has built for a kit. This may be a personal choice or a suggested model. The Scout should explain its features and have undertaken some research into the history and service of this type of aircraft.

competencies.statement: I can discuss with my Scouter (Hot Air Balloons,) how hot air balloons work and how to control them.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should discuss all aspects of hot air balloons. This can be done with the use of models. The Scout should understand the principle of hot air balloon flight.

competencies.statement: I know the rule relating to airfields.
competencies.explanation: Scouts should know the basic ‘Access to Airfields’ rules: Know the safe routes for getting around the airfield. Only enter airside areas if you have permission or a definite job to do. Understand the importance of keeping a good lookout at all times. Know how to recognise an active/ live aircraft. Know the correct way to approach an aircraft. Understand the dangers of propellers and jet engines and the danger areas associated with each.

competencies.statement: I understand how a wing derives lift.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how a wing works and how it lifts the plane.

competencies.statement: I can discuss with my Scouter Lift, Drag, Gravity and Thrust.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss with a Scouter how the four main forces of Lift, Drag, Gravity and Thrust work in aeronautics.

competencies.statement: I know the control surfaces of an aircraft.
competencies.explanation: Scouts should be able to identify the control surfaces on a diagram and describe how they move to control the path of flight of the aircraft to include: Ailerons. Elevators. Rudder.

competencies.statement: I can explain how an aero plane climbs, dives and turns using a model.
competencies.explanation: The Scout can use a model of any kind to explain the elements. This is a similar requirement to one in stage I but now we are seeking a deeper understanding of how a real plane climb, dives and turns.

competencies.statement: I can explain the causes of stalling.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should understand how stalling occurs. In explaining this they should refer to air speed, lift and how to recover from a stalling situation.

competencies.statement: I know the logos of the various airlines.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should have undertaken some research and be familiar with the common logos and livery of planes that fly in to Irish airspace. This requirement can be presented via a poster or perhaps a quiz. It can also be completed at an airport, giving direct observation of aircraft.

competencies.statement: I can build a Hot Air Balloon.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will have built a hot air balloon using a wire frame and tissue paper. Heat is provided by cotton wool in a small container. The Scout should discuss how they made the balloon and how it is inflated for flight. The balloon should then be launched. This can be done with the help of other members of their team.

competencies.statement: I have produced a project based on the Moon Landings.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should do a project on the Apollo Moon Landing and how it was achieved.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in a water rocket launch.
competencies.explanation: The Scout as a member of a team should undertake the construction of a water rocket. The launch can then take place in an open area as part of an activity.

competencies.statement: I understand what FOD is.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain what FOD stands for (foreign object damage) and how it applies to aircraft. The Scout should mention debris on the runway such as tyre rubber, birds in flight. Hazards at airfields that are near water and possible hazards from aircraft parts becoming dislodged inside and outside the aircraft.

competencies.statement: I know how to approach an aircraft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of how to act and behave on an airfield and discuss how they would approach an aircraft safely. Reference should be made to engines, pilot view and hand signals and communication with the pilot.

competencies.statement: I know the signs that an aircraft is about to start an engine.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be familiar with aircraft and how to behave around an airfield. The Scout should discuss signs of movement, engine noise, positioning of an aircraft. Checking of flaps etc.

competencies.statement: I know where the safe jet blast zones are on an aircraft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be familiar with aircraft and how to behave around an airfield. The Scout should discuss what a blast zone is and the dangers associated with it.

competencies.statement: I know how to identify different aircraft types from their features.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be familiar with a wide range of aircraft and be able to identify them parked on a runway, from pictures, in flight and from identification charts.

competencies.statement: I understand how weather affects air activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss in detail how weather affects flight – wind speed, cloud formation, icy conditions, thunder and lighting.

competencies.statement: I can show a younger Scout how control surfaces work.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be familiar with how control surfaces work and will be observed in action passing on such information to a younger Scout. The Scout should be encouraged to use models in passing on this information.

competencies.statement: I can build a scale model aircraft to a satisfactory standard from paper and balsa wood.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should present a scaled model for discussion. The model can be constructed from plans or from a kit and be painted in the correct colours as specified. The Scout should also talk about the build process, what they liked and difficulties they had.

competencies.statement: I can identify some aircraft instruments using a computer simulator, or other method.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be seated at a computer screen with a simulation game ready to be played. The Scout should bring the Scouter through the process of engaging with the game. The Scout should be able to identify some of the main instruments that comprise the panel and explain what they are used for.

competencies.statement: I can show how to take off and fly through various weather conditions and land safely using a computer simulator, or other method.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be seated at a computer screen with a simulation game ready to be played. The Scout should bring the Scouter through the process of engaging with the game. The Scout should be able to identify some of the main instruments that comprise the panel and explain what they are used for. Then when indicated they should take off, fly a course and land the plane. Various flying scenarios can be presented through the game setup.

competencies.statement: I can discuss with my Scouter how the Earth’s atmosphere affects air travel.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how the atmosphere has an impact on air travel and what are the various precautions that pilots have to take as a result.

competencies.statement: I can build and launch a water rocket.
competencies.explanation: The Scout as a member of their team should undertake the construction of a water rocket. The launch can then take place in an open area as part of an activity.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in at least two air activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will have taken part in a least two air activities. Ideally, these activities may have taken place at airfields that will facilitate learning for requirements above. However, they may also be air activities run locally by a Scout group.

competencies.statement: I can discuss aircraft navigation with my Scouter.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss how a pilot navigates when flying. This should include compass directions, land observation, air speed versus land speed and drift/drag and dead reckoning navigation.

competencies.statement: I know the types of air maps and the conventional signs used on them.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should discuss various map types and the conventional signs used on each. The Scout should also be able to show the differences between air maps and land based ordnance survey maps.

competencies.statement: I can demonstrate how to obtain a local forecast for an air activity.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how to get appropriate weather forecasts for flying and discuss the key points of a forecast that need to be noted and observed.

competencies.statement: I can explain how wind speed and direction are measured and how weather can affect various air activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss how a pilot navigates when flying. This should include compass directions, land observation, air speed versus land speed and drift/drag and dead reckoning navigation. The use of instruments and navigation aids.

competencies.statement: I can explain the difference between ground speed and air speed and how wind is used in takeoff and landing.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss how a plane takes off and how air and it’s speed moving over the surfaces of a wing provide lift. The Scout should then discuss the relationship between land speed and air speed in the context of travel through the air and it’s connection with navigation.

competencies.statement: I can discuss with my Scouter how the Earth’s atmosphere affects air travel.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss the air conditions as height is gained. Also the Scout should be able to discuss air pressure and gravity and how they affect flight.

competencies.statement: I can understand three different ways in which clouds are formed.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of how clouds are formed and how they affect flight and navigation. The Scout should talk about clouds in relation to mountain ranges, sea and high level clouds and stormy weather.

competencies.statement: I can show that I understand the basic ‘T’ instrument cluster.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of the T instrumental cluster and be able to name the key instruments that make up the cluster plus the likely instruments that will be ‘nearby’ or next to it. The Scout should be able to identify the altimeter, attitude meter, air speed, turn indicator and heading indicator.

competencies.statement: I can handle a powered model aircraft during takeoff and fly through various weather conditions and land safely.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be able to demonstrate this in an outdoor setting where his/her skill can be observed.

competencies.statement: I can explain the workings of aircraft pressure instruments, for example an altimeter or air speed indicator.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss how the instruments work internally. This might involve some research and the Scout might use pictures or drawings to explain their function.

competencies.statement: I can discuss how the Ionosphere affects communication.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how the Ionosphere – the uppermost part of the atmosphere has on communications and how its characteristics help with communication.

competencies.statement: I can navigate my patrol over a route using a GPS.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should devise an exercise (on the ground) in effect a route card and then using GPS compasses they should navigate to the points of the journey. They should be able to discuss accuracy of GPS devices over traditional compass methods.

competencies.statement: I have attended an Air Display.
I have participated in a themed ‘Space Camp’ or event with a group of Scouts.
I know the basic principles of a piston engine, including the four-stroke cycle.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of the different engines used on aircraft. Using charts, drawings or models the Scout should explain how the piston engine works.

competencies.statement: I know how a jet engine works.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of the different engines used on aircraft. Using charts, drawings or models the Scout should explain how a jet engine works.

competencies.statement: I know how rocket engines work, and their lift-off and re-entry procedures.
competencies.explanation: The Scout using charts, drawings or models should explain how a rocket engine works. The Scout should also discuss the lift –off procedures, safety and countdown checks. Re – entry procedures, checks, parachutes and drop zone. If they are discussing the space programme they should also talk about re-entry of shuttle, angle of descent.

competencies.statement: I know the Safety Code for Rocketry and able to identify the principal parts of a rocket.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be familiar with rockets and be involved in their construction so that they have detailed knowledge of the principle parts. As a rocket contains fuel it is vital that full safety procedures are followed in the construction phase and the take off and landing phase.

competencies.statement: I can build, launch, and recover a single or double-staged model rocket.
competencies.explanation: The Scout as a member of a team should undertake the construction of a single or double staged rocket model. The launch can then take place in an open area as part of an activity. It should be possible to recover this model for future flights.

competencies.statement: I know how to arrange permissions for a rocket launch.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should display an understanding that formal permissions need to be obtained to launch a fuel power rocket. The Scout should then explain the procedure of obtaining permissions from the appropriate authorities.

competencies.statement: I am able to fly a model aircraft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be able to demonstrate this in an outdoor setting where his/her skill can be observed.

competencies.statement: I can be responsible for planning a weekend camp for your group at an airfield.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be an experienced camper at this stage and be familiar with planning and organizing camps. In this case we are seeking an awareness of the extra requirements for a camp at an airfield. The Scout will draw from their experiences with Air Activities.

competencies.statement: I understand what a flight plan is.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should discuss how a flight plan is produced and what work is entailed in producing it. The Scout should also make connections with the production of a route card for a hike on the ground.

competencies.statement: I can produce a flight plan for a cross country exercise.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should produce a fully detailed flight plan for a cross country flight between two points specified by the Scouter before the requirement is worked on.

competencies.statement: I know the main types of checklists commonly found in aircraft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to describe in checklist fashion the formal checks that need to be undertaken before flight. Daily Inspection, Pre and Post flight.

competencies.statement: I know how to correctly approach an occupied aircraft or helicopter.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of how to act and behave on an airfield and discuss how they would approach an aircraft safely. Reference should be made to engines, pilot view and hand signals and communication with the pilot. With regards to helicopters – rotor span, downdraft and safe head height.

competencies.statement: I have a thorough knowledge of the Rule Relating to Airfields.
competencies.explanation: While the Scout maybe familiar with the basic rules relating to airfield at this level we expect the Scout to have an advanced and detailed knowledge of airfield, how to behave around them.

competencies.statement: I understand the Irish Air Traffic Control system.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be familiar with the Air Traffic Control system and methods. The Scout may also have visited a control tower and have practical experience and/or knowledge. They should also be familiar with radio communication, signs and call signs used by pilots and control towers to exchange information.

competencies.statement: I know how and when to use an air band radio.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be fully conversant with using air band radio and be able to talk about it. The Scout should be observed on a number of occasions using this equipment properly.

competencies.statement: I know how to marshal an aircraft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss the different signalling signs and what they mean. The Scout should then demonstrate their skill by marshalling an aircraft on an airfield.

competencies.statement: I have undertaken a project to demonstrate a particular aeronautical principle and build a suitable model to illustrate it.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will first indicate that they will undertake this requirement and discuss with the Scouter what they would like to do. Once completed the Scout should bring down the model to the section and display it.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in two air activity that got me airborne.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will have taken part in an air activity that has included air flight other than commercial flight. This will be done in conjunction with the Scouter and a flight instructor. The Scout should also be aware of insurance implications and parental permissions.

competencies.statement: I have planned a weekend camp for my section on an airfield.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be an experienced camper at this stage and be familiar with planning and organizing camps. In this case we are seeking an awareness of the extra requirements for a camp at an airfield. The Scout will draw from their experience in Air activities.

competencies.statement: I know the principle of flight of a helicopter.
I know the principle of flight of a helicopter.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will be able to discuss the main principles – lift, forward motion, turning, landing, torque, tail rotor, ground effect.

competencies.statement: I know how the controls of a helicopter work.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be fully aware of how a helicopter flies and how the controls differ from that of an aircraft. The Scout should discuss the use of collective, throttle, cyclic and anti-torque pedals, and how they are used in conjunction to fly the helicopter. The Scout should understand precession.

competencies.statement: I know the dangers regarding specific aerial activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to discuss a number of different air activities and the dangers or precautions that need to be taken to ensure a safe activity.

competencies.statement: I know how the constellation of satellites work to provide GPS navigation.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should run experiments into how the constellation of Satellites works in providing GPS navigation through its networking capabilities.

competencies.statement: I understand how telemetry helps develop aviation products.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of the impact of clear telemetry has on the development of aviation products and how information received using telemetry is used for aviation products.

competencies.statement: I have an understanding of Radar and how ATC use it.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should discuss how radar works and how to distinguish different signals on the screen. The Scout should then talk about the relationship between a pilot, air traffic control, flight plans, and the position of an aircraft in the sky in relation to other aircraft.

competencies.statement: I can arrange for a suitably experienced instructor to give an air experience flight.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will have taken part in an air activity that has included air flight other than commercial flight. This will be done in conjunction with the Scouter and a flight instructor. The Scout should also be aware of insurance implications and parental permissions.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in two different air activities that got me airborne.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will have taken part in an air activity that has included air flight other than commercial flight. This will be done in conjunction with the Scouter and a flight instructor. The Scout should also be aware of insurance implications and parental permissions.

skills.name: SI Paddling
skills.preface:
Requirements
Each of the skill requirements are presented as a statement of competency - I know how, I can
do, etc. These

competencies.statement: I have discussed what a wetsuit does.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know the dates when a wetsuit must be worn (Winter Season) and when it is optional (Summer Season). The Scout should have an idea how a wet suit works.

competencies.statement: I know what a buoyancy aid and life jacket are for.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know the main differences between a Standard Buoyancy Aid and a Life Jacket. The Scout should know when and where both Personal Floatation Devices (PFD’s) should be worn.

competencies.statement: I can show where the bow and stern are in a kayak or boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout is to be able to identify the difference between the Bow (Front) and Stern (Back) of a boat.

competencies.statement: I understand why I should follow directions from an instructor.
competencies.explanation: The Scout needs to discuss how to act in a boat. Know how to be aware of what’s happening around them and how to follow instructions from the Scouter in charge.

competencies.statement: I can show the limits of where I may go each time I go afloat for paddling.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be aware of the extent that they should go in a vessel and know any local dangers in the water.

competencies.statement: I know about the ‘Buddy’ system.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to talk about the buddy system and explain how and why it is used when in the water.

competencies.statement: I know why I should care for my wet suit, buoyancy aid and ‘cag’ after use.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know why it is important to wash their water activity equipment with cold fresh water after all usage.

competencies.statement: I know not go afloat if the wind is greater than Force 4.
I know how to contact the emergency services.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know the emergency number 112 (or 999) and say what kind of help is needed (Garda/Police, lifeboat, ambulance, fire brigade).

competencies.statement: I have taken part in a short exercise afloat.
competencies.explanation: A half day is at least two hours on or around the water.

competencies.statement: I can explain what special clothing and gear is to be worn and used while Kayaking.
competencies.explanation: The Scout must be able to describe what clothing must be worn while out paddling.

competencies.statement: I can put on my own Personal Flotation Device properly.
competencies.explanation: This should include securing all fastenings and using a crotch strap where it is fitted.

competencies.statement: Before I launch my boat, I can show where and when I am allowed to go.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know where it is safe to launch their boat. The Scout should know when it is safe to go onto the water.

competencies.statement: I have discussed ‘Weil’s’ disease and the precautions necessary to take in open water activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know where Weils disease can be contacted. The Scout should know the symptoms of Weil’s disease. The Scout should know how Weil’s disease is contracted. The Scout should know precautions to take from Weil’s disease. The Scout should know who is a risk from Weil’s disease.

competencies.statement: I have drawn a poster demonstrating the safety rules for swimming.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should draw up a poster to the best of their ability of their interpretation of the safety rules for swimming.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in an activity on safe enclosed waters involving paddling a Canadian canoe.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be briefed on safety procedures before starting the activity. The Scout should take part in a Paddling activity with the appropriate instructors present and in the suitable ratio and in safe enclosed waters. The activity should consist of two Canadian style canoes lashed together to form a catamaran. The activity shouldn’t go any more than 30 meters from the shore.

competencies.statement: I have discussed the appropriate action I should take in the case of a capsize.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the procedures to follow if they capsize in a kayak or a sit-on-top canoe.

competencies.statement: I have explained what impact I can have on local vegetation when launching and retrieving a boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain what impact they can have on the local vegetation when they are parking, changing and launching their boat. The Scout should explain how they can minimize impact on the natural environment. The Scout should explain how they would deal with wildlife if they were to come across it.

competencies.statement: I know how to raise the alarm if I see somebody in difficulty on the water.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know what department to call if you see someone in difficulty at sea. The Scout should know the number to call if you see someone in difficulty at sea. The Scout should know what the different colour safety flags mean on a beach.

competencies.statement: I know what hypothermia is.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know what is meant by the term hypothermia. The Scout should have a basic knowledge of the symptoms of hypothermia. The Scout should have a basic knowledge of how to treat hypothermia.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in at least two activities afloat.
competencies.explanation: A half day is at least two hours on or around the water.

competencies.statement: I can explain the importance of wearing the right clothing and gear while afloat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain why it is important to wear the correct clothing while out on the water.

competencies.statement: I can show how to test a raft for secure construction.
competencies.explanation: This should include ensuring buoyancy is firmly in place and that all lashings are secure.

competencies.statement: I know how to do CPR and place a victim in the recovery position.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to demonstrate an up-to-date CPR technique on a suitable mannequin and demonstrate how to put an adult or child in the recovery position (also known as the safe-airway position).

competencies.statement: I know how to make use of a paddle while on a raft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how to use a paddle while paddling a triangular course set down by their leader.

competencies.statement: I know what to do in the case of a capsize/ or raft breakup and the procedures to follow.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain what actions should be taken in case they end up in the water while boating and rafting.

competencies.statement: I know how to tie and when to use the following knots.Round-turn-and-two-half-hitches,Figure of eight, Bowline, Reef knot, Clove Hitch.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to tie the list of knots above. The Scout should be able to explain what the knots are for and give examples of their practical uses.

competencies.statement: I can tie a square lashing.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate how to tie a square lashing using rope and spars.

competencies.statement: I know how and where to get the latest weather forecast for the area I will be paddling in.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain four ways of getting the most recent forecast for the area they are paddling in.

competencies.statement: I can make a recognised distress signal.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how to signal for help when out on the water.

competencies.statement: I know that I should follow the instructions of the person in charge of the boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout may be asked to explain what a charge certificate is and why it is important that the person in charge of activities afloat should be suitably qualified.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in making a simple raft for four people.
competencies.explanation: As part of a team build a raft and paddle it on a triangular course set out by the leader.

competencies.statement: I can explain why wearing the correct outerwear is important.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain that outerwear protects from both getting wet in rain and from the effects of wind-chill.

competencies.statement: I can assist in the launch and recover of a raft.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should take part in an activity where they help build a raft, float it and recover.

competencies.statement: I know the safety precautions required for water based activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know what safety precautions to take before and during water based activity.

competencies.statement: I know the main points of ‘Leave No Trace’.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know the principles behind ‘Leave no Trace’.

competencies.statement: I can work as part of a team to paddle a raft on a triangular course.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should take part in building a raft for four people and paddle it through a triangular course set down by their leader. The Scout should be able to explain what the knots are for and give examples of their practical use.

competencies.statement: I can demonstrate how to whip a ropes end and then show how to coil the rope.
competencies.explanation: No whipping is specified but it should be secure and appropriate for the cordage. The Scout should demonstrate how to coil a rope properly. Rope should be no less than 15 meters long.

competencies.statement: I know the Beaufort wind scale up to Force 6.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the visual clues used to estimate the wind strength.

competencies.statement: I can demonstrate throwing a throw line to a casualty, preparing the rope for the throw and instructing the casualty to use the rope.
competencies.explanation: Heave the causality to shore. This can be demonstrated in open water or a swimming pool. From land, the scout should demonstrate throwing a throw line to a target approx 10 meters away on a lake, beach or lagoon.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in and logged at least four rafting activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should have taken part and logged four rafting activities which include planning, building and paddling a raft.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in three activities on safe enclosed waters involving paddling a Canadian canoe.
competencies.explanation: A half day is at least two hours on or around the water.

competencies.statement: I know the difference between winter and summer Kayaking.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know Scouting Irelands dates for summer time boating and winter time boating. The Scout should know the difference between being out on the water in winter and summer.

competencies.statement: An understanding of the basic safety rules of canoeing.
competencies.explanation: You must be able to swim. You must always wear a buoyancy aid. You must always ensure that there is adequate kayak buoyancy. You must never canoe alone.

competencies.statement: An ability to enter and exit a kayak correctly.
competencies.explanation: Entry and exit with or without the use of a paddle is acceptable.

competencies.statement: Forward Paddle, Reverse Paddle, and Stop.
competencies.explanation: Veering is allowed for, but a participant must be able to maintain reasonable directional stability for at least 25 metres. A Scout should demonstrate an ability to stop when moving forward and in reverse.

competencies.statement: An ability to turn while stationary using forward sweep stroke, reverse sweep stroke and a combination of forward and reverse sweep strokes.
competencies.explanation: There should be an efficient use of the paddle in turning and stopping the kayak.

competencies.statement: Capsize Drill Assessment.
competencies.explanation: The capsize and exit from the kayak, should be carried out in water of sufficient depth adjacent to the shore/bank. The use of a spray deck is optional.

competencies.statement: General aims Stage 6 aims to enable Scouts to kayak safely and competently on flat water and Grade I Rivers as a member of a group.
competencies.explanation: Assist in basic rescues. Foster further participation in canoeing.

competencies.statement: Simple draw stroke.
competencies.explanation: A Scout must demonstrate correctly. All strokes should be demonstrated in relevant situations i.e. use of a simple draw stroke to manoeuvre the kayak to the bank. Strokes should be demonstrated on both sides of the kayak.

competencies.statement: Low brace.
competencies.explanation: A Scout must demonstrate correctly. All strokes should be demonstrated in relevant situations. Strokes should be demonstrated on both sides of the kayak.

competencies.statement: Low brace turn.
competencies.explanation: A Scout must demonstrate correctly. All strokes should be demonstrated in relevant situations. Strokes should be demonstrated on both sides of the kayak.

competencies.statement: Edging while the kayak is moving.
competencies.explanation: A Scout must demonstrate correctly. All strokes should be demonstrated in relevant situations. Strokes should be demonstrated on both sides of the kayak.

competencies.statement: Capsize drill.
competencies.explanation: A Scout must demonstrate correctly. A spray deck must be worn throughout an assessment.

competencies.statement: An ability to assist in an H rescue, and in an assisted X rescue.
competencies.explanation: Some role to fulfil in the completion of these rescues.

competencies.statement: General aims Stage 7 aims to enable Scouts to kayak safely and competently on river up to and including Grade II rivers as a member of a group.
competencies.explanation: Be capable of negotiating obstacles likely to be encountered on Grade II rivers. Assist in rescues. Foster further participation in canoeing.

competencies.statement: Strokes.
competencies.explanation: Scouts must successfully explain and demonstrate the following techniques and skills at a level higher than that required for stage 6. Forward paddle, Reverse paddle, Emergency stop, Forward sweep, Reverse sweep and a combination of forward and reverse sweep. Draw stroke, Sculling draw, Hanging draw, Sculling for support, Low brace, High brace, Low brace turn, Stern rudder, Bow rudder. All strokes should be demonstrated in relevant situations i.e. sculling in a small stopper. Strokes should be demonstrated on both sides of the kayak.

competencies.statement: Techniques.
competencies.explanation: Scouts must successfully explain and demonstrate the following techniques and skills at a level higher than that required for stage 6. Entry and exit, Edging, Forward ferry gliding, Reverse ferry gliding, Breaking in, Breaking out, Capsize drill. Entry and Exit can be carried out with or without the use of paddles, depending on what is most appropriate to the situation.

competencies.statement: Rescues.
competencies.explanation: Scouts must successfully explain and demonstrate the following techniques and skills at a level higher than that required for stage 6. Assisted X rescue, an X rescue, Eskimo rescue and Eskimo roll. An understanding of the use of defensive swimming. Generally, required assessment rescues will be kept until the end of an assessment.

competencies.statement: Theory - Safety Rules.
competencies.explanation: Demonstrate an understanding of Eddies, Standing waves, V waves, Stoppers, and Easy river routes i.e. the main flow down a Grade rapid. An understanding of good control (i.e. responding to various signals and commands).

competencies.statement: Assessment.
competencies.explanation: During an assessment a Scout must explain and demonstrate all techniques and skills at a level higher than previously demonstrated. All techniques, skills and rescues must be demonstrated to an assessor’s satisfaction in order to achieve this award. No part of an assessment can be taken in a swimming pool. All assessment criteria must be demonstrated outdoors on water of Grade II difficulty as part of a river trip. Scouts undertaking this award must be at least 12 years of age.

competencies.statement: General aims Stage 8 aims to enable Scouts to kayak safely and proficiently on rivers up to and including Grade III difficulty.
competencies.explanation: Be capable of negotiating obstacles likely to be encountered on Grade III River. Deal competently with rescue situations that might occur on rivers up to and including Rivers of Grade III difficulty. Develop group awareness.

competencies.statement: Strokes- I can demonstrate successfully.
competencies.explanation: To obtain stage 8 the Scout must successfully explain and demonstrate the following techniques and skills at a level higher than that required for the stage 7 and be capable of demonstrating any combination of the strokes competently and efficiently. The assessment will take place during a river trip of at least three miles on water of Grade III difficulty. Forward paddle, Reverse paddle, Emergency stop. Forward sweep, Reverse sweep and a combination of forward and reverse sweep, Edging, Bow rudder, Stern rudder, Low brace turn, Low recovery, High recovery, Sculling for support, Sculling draw, Draw stroke, Hanging draw, Defensive swimming.

competencies.statement: Techniques- I can demonstrate.
competencies.explanation: An ability to use water conditions available for the effective and efficient manoeuvring of a kayak. Competence in negotiating water obstructions i.e. Standing Waves, Stoppers, and an ability to utilize it to cross a river. Competence in negotiating bends where water flows under trees or against vertical riverbank. Forward ferry gliding (facing upriver), Reverse ferry gliding (facing downriver). Breaking in accurately, Breaking out accurately. Eskimo roll, Capable of self-rescue.

competencies.statement: Rescues and Safety Techniques.
competencies.explanation: Assisted X and/or an X rescue. Eskimo rescue (maximum lower body rotation), Curl rescue and/or TX rescue, Stern carry. Unconscious casualty (method of righting an unconscious person in a capsized kayak). An ability to manoeuvre an empty kayak between two specified points. An ability to assist an incapacitate paddler in a kayak between two specified points. An ability to use a throw rope to rescue a swimmer and have a practical knowledge of First Aid. This should extend to possible situations arising during a canoeing trip to include: Shock, Hypothermia, Head injuries, Dislocations, Bleeding, CPR, EAR.

competencies.statement: Theory-An understanding of the following.
competencies.explanation: River grading, River route finding, Types of GP kayaks and paddles, Towing systems and methods, Group control and awareness, Signals and commands, Personal equipment.

competencies.statement: Deal competently with rescue situations which might occur on rivers up to and including rivers of Grade 4 & advanced white water difficulty.
Deal competently with First Aid situations in the river environment.
Demonstrate a thorough knowledge of safety precautions and procedures to be adopted while with a group on Grade 4 & advanced White Water Rivers.
Demonstrate an ability to assess a group’s competence to deal with conditions likely to be encountered on Grade 4 & advanced White Water Rivers.
Demonstrate an ability to command trust from a group of peers while on rivers of Grade 4 & advanced white water.
Demonstrate the necessary skills to communicate effectively with other group members on Grade 4 & advanced white water rivers.
Deal efficiently with rescue situations likely to occur on Grade 4 & advanced white water rivers.
Demonstrate a constant awareness of other group members, their location on the river and within the group.
Demonstrate a sufficient knowledge of the river’s environs.
Demonstrate an ability to read white water to a high standard.
Present a suitable and correctly fitted out kayak and other appropriate equipment.
competencies.explanation: It would be expected that equipment be of a standard consistent with the responsibilities of being part of a group undertaking a trip on a Grade 4 & advanced White Water River. Equipment should be readily accessible at all times. Examination of equipment will form an important part of the overall assessment. (see Stage 9 Equipment List over leaf).

skills.name: SI Rowing
skills.preface:
Requirements
Each of the skill requirements are presented as a statement of competency - I know how, I
can do, etc. These

competencies.statement: I can assist in the launching of a small punt.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should assist in the launching in an age appropriate way. The scout should be aware of the need to be careful around water.

competencies.statement: I know about the buddy system.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to talk about the buddy system and explain how and why it is used when in the water.

competencies.statement: I know the importance of a personal floatation device.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know that wearing a personal floatation device is important around water and how they should not go near any boat without first having a personal flotation device on them.

competencies.statement: I know the correct clothing to wear when going afloat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to show footwear and layers of light clothing suitable for boating. A windproof jacket of some sort should also be worn.

competencies.statement: I can row a small punt.
competencies.explanation: Depending on the age of the Scout it may be considered prudent to have a competent person in the boat too. The Scout should be able to propel the punt with some directional control.

competencies.statement: I can point out the bow, stern, transom, bowline, port and starboard of a boat, rudder, oar.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to name the parts when pointed to and point to the named parts.

competencies.statement: I know how to contact the emergency services.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know the emergency number 112 (or 999) and say what kind of help is needed (Garda/Police, lifeboat, ambulance, fire brigade).

competencies.statement: I know why it is important to stay with a capsized boat.
competencies.explanation: A capsized boat is easier to see in the water than a head and the hull will help you stay afloat.

competencies.statement: I know why I should follow directions from my instructor.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should understand how to behave on a boat and that there may be safety reason why an instructor doesn’t have time to explain a direction in advance.

competencies.statement: I know not go afloat if the wind is greater than Force 4.
I can show the limits of where I may go each time I go afloat.
competencies.explanation: A Scout should know that for safety reasons they should stay within a defined area. They should know how far they can go.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in two half-day exercises afloat.
competencies.explanation: A half day is at least two hours on or around the water.

competencies.statement: I can assist in the launch and recovery of a small punt.
competencies.explanation: This should include making sure there is no water in the punt when it is put away.

competencies.statement: I can explain what impact I may have on local vegetation when launching and retrieving a punt.
competencies.explanation: Use a slipway where possible, avoid launching in or near nesting sites and where vegetation will be trampled down and damaged.

competencies.statement: I have discussed “Weil’s disease” and the precautions necessary to take part in open water activities.
competencies.explanation: Avoiding stagnant water and canal banks, proper personal hygiene before and after going afloat and covering open wounds with a water-proof plaster.

competencies.statement: I can put on my own personal floatation device properly.
competencies.explanation: This should include securing all fastenings and using a crotch strap where it is fitted.

competencies.statement: I know why I should wear suitable footwear.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain that it offers better grip, warmth and protection from sharp protrusions as well as debris in the water.

competencies.statement: I can make a recognised distress signal.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to make one of the signals described in the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea.

competencies.statement: I know how to raise the alarm if I see somebody in difficulty on the water.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know how to make a call to the emergency services and give clear information as to what was seen and where.

competencies.statement: I know what hypothermia is.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should have a knowledge of the signs and symptoms of hypothermia and have an understanding of why it is a problem.

competencies.statement: I know that I should keep clear of channels and fairways.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to identify channels and fairways in their local boating waters and understand why other boats may not be able to avoid a scout in a punt.

competencies.statement: I can get a weather forecast.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to get a local or national weather forecast suitable for outdoor activity.

competencies.statement: I can tie the following knots; Round-turn-and-two-half-hitches, Figure of eight, Bowline.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to tie the named knots on request.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in four half-day exercises afloat.
competencies.explanation: A half day is at least two hours on or around the water.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in the launch and recovery of a small rowing punt.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to direct other Scouts as to how and where to launch and recover the boat including ensuring that the boat is bailed fully before being stored.

competencies.statement: I can put on my personal floatation device and adjust it properly.
competencies.explanation: Many PFDs are adjustable. The Scout should be able to make appropriate adjustments in order that the PFD fits the scout correctly.

competencies.statement: I know why wearing layers of clothing is a good idea.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the benefit of a layered approach and identify clothing best suited as a base, mid or top layer.

competencies.statement: I can embark, manoeuvre and disembark from a rowing punt safely.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to demonstrate an ability to get in and out of a punt safely, row in a straight line and demonstrate an ability to turn, stop, reverse and come alongside in a controlled manner. The Scout should be able to carry out these manoeuvres alone or with others onboard.

competencies.statement: I can point out the parts of a boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be familiar with and be able to name and point out thwarts, gunwale, spur/oarlock and rowlock as well as those parts previously mentioned.

competencies.statement: I can use a small anchor from a punt.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to set up, tie in, deploy and recover a suitably sized anchor.

competencies.statement: I can get into the water from a punt in a safe way.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate a suitable technique which is safe for the type of craft in use. The transom would usually be considered the safest place to do this.

competencies.statement: I can help to right a capsized rowing punt.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to follow direction to assist in the righting of a capsized rowing punt.

competencies.statement: I know how to do CPR and place the casualty in the recovery position.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to demonstrate an up-to-date CPR technique on a suitable mannequin and demonstrate how to put an adult or child in the recovery position (also known as the safe-airway position).

competencies.statement: I know that I should follow the instructions of the person in charge of the boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout may be asked to explain what a charge certificate is and why it is important that the person in charge of activities afloat should be suitably qualified.

competencies.statement: I understand the terms that are used in a maritime weather forecast.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the following terms and what they mean in the context of a maritime weather forecast; small craft warning, gale warning, imminent, soon, later.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in three full day exercises afloat.
competencies.explanation: A full day afloat shall involve not less than four hours in or around a boat. This may include a lunch break. The scout will not be expected to be rowing all the time. At this stage a Scout would be expected to row as a member of the crew of a suitable rowing boat such as the Sea Scout standard boat (BP18). Oars should be of a size suitable for the crew rowing.

competencies.statement: I can assist in the launch and recovery of a rowing boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should now be able to take a useful place as a member of the larger team needed to launch and recover a larger rowing boat. They should be aware of the need for care when lifting heavy objects and the importance of co-ordinated action to avoid injury.

competencies.statement: I know the main principles of “Leave No Trace”.
I know that there are different types of personal floatation device and know when and where each should be used.
competencies.explanation: The Scouting Ireland Boating Guidelines recommend different standards of PFD (50N, 100N, 150N, 275N) for use in different circumstances.

competencies.statement: I can explain why wearing the correct outerwear is important.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain that outerwear protects from both getting wet in rain and from the effects of wind-chill.

competencies.statement: I can carry out boat manoeuvres as a member of the crew in a rowing boat.
competencies.explanation: As a member of the crew a Scout should be able to embark and disembark safely and react appropriately to the various commands; sight spur/ oar, toss oars, ship oars, boat oars, give way, back water, hold water, trail oars.

competencies.statement: I can point out the parts of a boat.
competencies.explanation: As in previous stages plus, yoke, tiller, pintle, gudgeon, strake, rib.

competencies.statement: I can pick up a mooring from a punt.
competencies.explanation: Rowing in a punt unaccompanied the scout should be able to approach a mooring appropriately, pick up the mooring and secure it to the boat in a safe and seamanlike manner.

competencies.statement: I can help another person safely into a punt from the water.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to approach the casualty in the water and, by using a combination of lifting and moving their own body weight, assist another person in to the punt from the water.

competencies.statement: I can coil a line and heave it to a casualty to affect a simulated rescue.
competencies.explanation: This should be done with a suitable weighted, floating line over a distance of at least 10m, bringing the casualty safely to shore.

competencies.statement: I know the safety precautions required for water based activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain Weather, Area, Tides, Clothing, Hull, Inventory, Tell Someone.

competencies.statement: I know the Beaufort wind scale up to force 6.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know the wind speeds related to the Beaufort scale, estimate the force from visual clues (waves, trees, smoke) and understand the significance of a “Small Craft Warning” in the weather forecast.

competencies.statement: I can describe how often high and low tides take place, and the implications these might when going afloat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the impact of the tide on the local boating waters. Such concerns as strong tidal flow and inaccessible moorings are relevant here.

competencies.statement: I know that where I may go boating may change in different conditions.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should understand that different areas may be safer in different wind directions and strengths.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in six full-day exercises afloat.
competencies.explanation: A full day could involve a journey such as on a river or canal, for example during a summer camp.

competencies.statement: I know the standard rowing commands used in my group and can use them to helm a rowing boat on a straight course.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to use a range of commands such as “Easy, Port” or “Hard, together” rather than being overly reliant on large rudder movements or “Hold water” turns.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading role in mooring and unmooring a rowing boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to direct a crew to safely pick up and cast off a mooring.

competencies.statement: I can assist in the anchoring of a rowing boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be capable of setting up the anchor, ensuring it is secured to the boat and deploying it overboard as directed by the coxswain.

competencies.statement: I can identify and name the main parts of common anchor types.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to name the principle parts of a Fisherman or Admiralty anchor, a ploughshare style anchor and a fluke style anchor.

competencies.statement: I know why it is important to have some training in first aid and can show how to care for someone who is very cold.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the importance of having first aid training and demonstrate an ability to treat a casualty showing signs of hypothermia. It is desirable that a scout have some formal training in first aid.

competencies.statement: I know the parts of the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea which apply to my boat and local boating waters.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain which is the stand on vessel and which is the give way vessel in situations involving overtaking, crossing tracks and head on situations between rowing boats, rowing and sailing boats and between rowing boats and power boats. The Scout should also be able to explain correct procedure in and around channels and fairways.

competencies.statement: I can obtain a weather forecast and know how the information might affect planned activities afloat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to obtain a suitable, up to date marine weather forecast for the relevant area and interpret how that forecast might alter plans.

competencies.statement: I know how currents and the ebb and flow of the tide affect my local boating waters.
I know the use of Channel 16 on marine VHF and have an understanding of the use of distress flares.
I have taken part in 6 full-day exercises afloat.
I have taken part in one expedition afloat.
competencies.explanation: An expedition is an extended journey afloat involving either camping ashore or sleeping aboard. The inland waterways of Ireland offer many opportunities for such expeditions.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in the launch and recovery of a rowing boats.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to direct others in launching and recovering a rowing boat. This may be with or without the use of a trailer or trolley. The Scout should ensure proper manual handling procedure is observed and that care is taken to prevent strain and crushing injuries.

competencies.statement: I can carry out the routine inspection of a personal floatation device.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate how to inspect a PFD for visual flaws such as tears, failed stitching, defective fastenings.

competencies.statement: I can take the helm of a rowing boat and carry out manoeuvres including steering with a compass.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to take the helm of a multi-oared rowing boat and get underway, demonstrate control of the boat and crew and turn to port and starboard, pick up a mooring, pass between obstacles such as moored boats, make way astern and come alongside safely.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in anchoring a rowing boat including knowing how and when to use a tripping line.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to direct another Scout in ensuring the anchor is correctly set up, that the line is secured to the boat and not fouled and that they are anchoring in a suitable place. The Scout should explain the use of a tripping line.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in Man-Over-Board exercise.
competencies.explanation: The Scout will have taken part in a Man-Over-Board exercise with a live casualty or a suitable substitute. They should have experience as a crew member, and possibly as casualty so that they will better understand the difficulties in locating and recovering a casualty.

competencies.statement: I know what causes tides and how spring and neap tides might affect sailors.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain the interaction of the sun and moon and explain the increase in both tidal range and tidal rate during spring tides.

competencies.statement: I can recognise the main weather patterns illustrated by a synoptic chart and can interpret the forecast.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to look at a synoptic weather chart and use it to make their own weather forecast. For a given verbal weather forecast they should be able to interpret the terms used and describe the weather to be expected especially in terms of wind speed and direction and visibility.

competencies.statement: I can identify common weather conditions and describe how they may affect boating activities.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to describe the main weather features to expect with high or low pressure and with warm and cold fronts.

competencies.statement: I am familiar with the main features of restricted waters as defined for my group.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to describe the extent of Restricted Waters as defined for their group and identify headlands and any ports of refuge that might exist.

competencies.statement: I know how and when to make Distress and Urgency calls and Safety Announcements on Marine VHF.
I have taken part in eight full-day exercises afloat.
I have taken part in one expedition afloat.
I have instructed at least four people in four of the areas up to stage 3.
I can take a leading part in the manual handling of a rowing boat ashore ensuring safe handling procedures.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to direct a group of scouts handling a rowing boat ashore. The boat may be on a trailer or trolley or it may be carried. The scout should show an awareness of potential risk to the boat, the scouts and members of the public who may be in the area.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in preparing a rowing boat for safe transportation.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to direct others in putting the boat on the trailer and securing it with rope or straps. Ultimately responsibility for trailer suitability and load security must still lie with the driver of the towing vehicle.

competencies.statement: I know under which circumstances different Personal Flotation Devices are appropriate.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to explain where and when the Scouting Ireland Boating Guidelines advise the use of different types of PFD.

competencies.statement: I can take charge of a rowing boat and carry out the required manoeuvres, including towing, to a high standard.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to act as coxswain of a multi-oared rowing boat and carry out all the manoeuvres required in the previous stage. A greater degree of control is to be expected and the Scout should be able to manoeuvre between obstacles that require the trailing of oars. The Scout should also demonstrate an ability to take another similarly sized boat under tow and tow it to safety.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in selecting a good anchorage.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to select a suitable anchorage given due acknowledgement to sea bed, scope, shelter and sea.

competencies.statement: I can take charge of a boat and respond efficiently to a (simulated) emergency.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to react calmly and efficiently to a simulated emergency such as MOB or the loss of an oar ensuring a safe and orderly recovery. The Scout should make it clear that they understand they are in charge of the crew as well as the boat.

competencies.statement: I know what lights should be shown by the most common vessels in my area and know what lights should be shown by a rowing boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to identify from sight or pictures, the nature of a vessel showing particular lights and describe what the vessel is doing. (crossing, head-on, overtaking...) The Scout should also be able to describe what lights are required on a rowing boat according to the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea.

competencies.statement: I know the relevant sections of the International regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea.
I can interpret the current forecast and make sound decisions on planned activities in view of expected weather and sea conditions and tidal effects.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate their ability to use weather forecasting information in planning activities afloat including knowing when to cancel an activity.

competencies.statement: I know the hazards and how the weather may affect “Restricted Waters” for my group.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to describe hazards such as rocks, tidal races, shipping lanes and overfalls which may exist in Restricted Waters as defined for their group. The Scout should also be able to describe how different wind directions may affect the area. Onshore and offshore winds may be of particular importance here.

competencies.statement: I know how to get suitable information for “Safe Enclosed” boating waters that are not my groups local waters (e.g. for camp).
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to identify suitable people to ask for information such as lifeboat crew, fishermen and the coast guard and know what type of information they need to get.

competencies.statement: I can assist in developing a passage plan for a day trip.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to help others to make a plan bearing in mind wind, tides and currents, the ability of the crew, the nature of the craft and availability of rescue cover and suitable stopping places. Lights, landmarks and hazards along the route would be considered an essential part of the plan.

competencies.statement: I know how to read and set a chart, plot and estimate positions.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to use maritime charts and demonstrate an understanding of position marking conventions.

competencies.statement: I have a working knowledge of GMDSS as it applies to EPIRBs and DSC.
I have taken part in ten full-day exercises afloat.
I have taken part in 1 overnight expedition afloat outside my normal boating waters.
I have instructed at least four people in at least six of the areas up to Stage 5.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should chose six of the twelve topics listed for Stage 5 of the Rowing Adventure skills and instruct them to the required standard.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in the safe manual handling of rowing boat ashore including turning them over.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to direct others in all areas of handling rowing boats ashore. When turning a boat over the scout should demonstrate due caution for the Scouts doing the lifting as well as the boat and surrounding property.

competencies.statement: I can take a leading part in organising the off- season storage of rowing boats.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate how best to store boats in the off season. This should include suitable covers for boats stored outdoors, placing boats so as not to obstruct access and emergency walkways and appropriate support of the boat to prevent damage to the boat.

competencies.statement: I understand the different safety precautions that must be taken when a group of boats is operating together.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an understanding of the different problems that can arise with multi-craft activities. This might include differences in performance or crew ability and the additional communications requirements to ensure boats do not become too far separated.

competencies.statement: I have a good understanding of the merits of different anchor types for different locations and conditions.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain the merits of different types of anchor in different circumstances and identify the type of anchor best suited to local waters. This may require identifying more than one type of anchor if different seabed conditions exist in various parts of the groups Day Cruising waters.

competencies.statement: I know what sound signals the most common types of vessel in my area should make.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate knowledge of the various sound signals (fog signals and general sound signals for manoeuvring) that may be used by the types of vessels the Scout is likely to encounter in the groups Day Cruising Waters.

competencies.statement: I have researched at least five pieces of weather lore.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate knowledge of at least five pieces of weather lore (Red sky at night..., spiders spinning webs...). Their knowledge should include an evaluation as to how useful any piece of weather lore might be in predicting the local weather.

competencies.statement: I am familiar with ‘Day Cruising Waters’ for my group.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate a knowledge of the extent of Day Cruising Waters for their group and the various features of it including, but not limited to; ports of refuge, man-made and natural hazards, shipping lanes and channels.

competencies.statement: I can use the information from a charts etc., to plan an expedition in restricted waters.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should use information from published and informal sources to produce an expedition plan. This plan would include launch and recovery sites, camp sites, sources of fresh water and supplies, tidal streams and ranges, ports of refuge, emergency plans, inventory lists etc.

competencies.statement: I have an understanding of the ‘capture effect’ as it applies to marine VHF.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain their understanding of the Capture effect and how it may impact on communications.

competencies.statement: I have taken part in 10 full-day exercises afloat.
I have taken part in one overnight expedition involving more than one boat.
I have instructed at least four people in at least seven of the areas up to Stage 6.
I can take a leading part in preparing a rowing boat for transportation by road including identifying a suitable trailer/vehicle and secure the boat safely.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate some awareness of legal issues regarding road trailers (lights, brakes) as well as the weight capacity of the trailer. If a commercial vehicle is to be used the Scout should demonstrate an ability to give consideration to suitable cradling of the boat to ensure its safe transportation.

competencies.statement: I have knowledge of the organising of rowing races for boats of the type used by my group.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate knowledge of how to go about organising a rowing race. Consideration should be given to a fair start and turns, adequate rescue cover, equal lanes and a straight finish line. The Scout should also demonstrate a knowledge of any class rules concerning design, dimensions and modifications.

competencies.statement: I can anchor a boat efficiently to two anchors.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to lay a boat to two anchors either for added security or to reduce scope.

competencies.statement: I can improvise and deploy a sea-anchor and know what spares and tools should be carried aboard.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should explain what spares and tools should be carried aboard in safe enclose, restricted or day cruising waters. The Scout should also demonstrate an ability to improvise a sea-anchor from materials which could be expected aboard a rowing boat. The Scout should explain when and why to use a sea-anchor.

competencies.statement: I have completed the requirement for the Emergencies Skills Stage 7.
I know how to interact with the emergency services.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate knowledge of how to communicate with the emergency services using both communications technology and visual signals. The Scout should demonstrate an understanding of what information the emergency services might need in an emergency situation.

competencies.statement: I know what sound signals the most common types of vessel in my area should make. I can identify the type aspect and behaviour of vessels by day or night from lights, shapes and sounds.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate their knowledge of lights, day shapes and sounds and what information they give regarding the vessel.

competencies.statement: I know the procedure for entry to and departure from a harbour and understand the requirement to file a passage plan under SOLAS regulations.

I can complete a rough synoptic chart from a maritime weather forecast or similar data and use this information to make sound decisions on planned activities in view of expected weather and sea conditions.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate an ability to construct an approximate synoptic chart from the data given in the wide area shipping forecast broadcast by the BBC. This chart should give the approximate position of any cyclones and anti-cyclones as well as any weather fronts.

competencies.statement: I am familiar with any local rules and bylaws that apply to Day Cruising Waters for my group.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should demonstrate their knowledge of any rules any bylaws concerning boating in Day Cruising Waters. This may include areas of restricted activity, speed limits, restrictions on times of operation and craft given stand-on privilege, among others.

competencies.statement: I can devise a pilot/passage plan and programme that plan into a GPS.
I have taken part in ten full-day exercises afloat.
I have taken part in an overnight expedition in coastal waters.
I have instructed at least four people in at least five of the areas up to stage 8.

skills.name: SI Sailing
skills.preface:
Requirements
Each of the skill requirements are presented as a statement of competency - I know how, I can do, etc.
These

competencies.statement: I can assist with the launch and recovery of a sailing dinghy.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should assist in the launching in an age appropriate way. The scout should be aware of the need to be careful around water.

competencies.statement: I know about the Buddy system.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to talk about the buddy system and explain how and why it is used when in the water.

competencies.statement: I know the importance of a personal floatation device.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should know that wearing a personal floatation device is important around water and how they should not go near any boat without first having a personal floatation device on them.

competencies.statement: I know the correct clothing to wear when sailing.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to show footwear and layers of light clothing suitable for boating. A windproof jacket of some sort should also be worn. The scout should be able to put on a wet suit with help.

competencies.statement: I can take the helm and steer a reasonably straight course.
competencies.explanation: Depending on the age of the Scout it may be considered prudent to have a competent person in the boat too. The Scout should be demonstrating some directional control.

competencies.statement: I know not go afloat if the wind is greater than Force 4.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should understand that it is unwise to go afloat if it is too windy.

competencies.statement: I can point out the bow, stern, port and starboard of a boat.
competencies.explanation: The Scout should be able to name the parts when pointed to and point to the named parts.

competencies.statement: I know how to contact the emergency services.
